function.description: Generates a comprehensive report based on user activity data within a specified time frame. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

user_id.description: The unique identifier for the user.

start_date.description: The start date for the report period in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

end_date.description: The end date for the report period, inclusive, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

include_inactive.description: Flag to determine if inactive users should be included in the report.

report_format.description: The format in which the report will be generated.

**Ionisation methods – a quick guide** | Ionisation technique | Typical application | Key advantages | Common limitations | |----------------------|---------------------|----------------|--------------------| | **Electron Impact (EI)** | Gas‑phase mass spectrometry (GC‑MS) | • Simple, robust;
• Produces reproducible fragmentation patterns;
• Good for volatile, thermally stable compounds | • Requires high vacuum;
• Not suitable for large, labile molecules | | **Chemical Ionisation (CI)** | GC‑MS, some LC‑MS | • Softer than EI → less fragmentation;
• Useful for larger, polar molecules | • Still needs GC‑compatible analytes;
• Lower sensitivity for very polar species | | **Photoionisation (PI)** | GC‑MS, some LC‑MS | • Non‑destructive, soft ionisation;
• Can be tuned with wavelength | • Requires UV source;
• Limited to molecules with suitable ionisation energy | | **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** | LC‑MS, proteomics, metabolomics | • Soft, handles large biomolecules;
• Operates at atmospheric pressure;
• Produces multiply charged ions → lower m/z | • Requires aqueous or polar solvents;
• Susceptible to ion suppression | | **Matrix‑Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI)** | Proteomics, polymers, large biomolecules | • Very soft;
• Handles high‑molecular‑weight analytes;
• Fast analysis | • Requires matrix;
• Less quantitative;
• Limited to solid samples | | **Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)** | LC‑MS, small molecules | • Good for moderately polar compounds;
• Works with non‑polar solvents | • Less effective for highly polar analytes | | **Atmospheric Pressure Photoionisation (APPI)** | LC‑MS, non‑polar compounds | • Soft ionisation for non‑polar species;
• Works with a wide solvent range | • Requires UV lamp;
• Less common than ESI/APCI | | **Laser Ablation Ionisation (LAI)** | Surface analysis, solid samples | • Direct sampling;
• Minimal sample prep | • Requires laser system;
• Limited to surface‑accessible analytes | | **Field Ionisation (FI)** | High‑resolution MS, large molecules | • Extremely soft;
• Produces singly charged ions | • Requires high vacuum;
• Low throughput | ### Choosing the “best” method 1. **Sample type & state** - *Volatile, thermally stable*: EI or CI (GC‑MS). - *Large biomolecules (proteins, peptides)*: ESI or MALDI (LC‑MS). - *Non‑polar, high‑molecular‑weight polymers*: MALDI or FI. - *Polar, small metabolites*: ESI or APCI. 2. **Desired information** - *Structural elucidation*: EI (fragmentation) or ESI with tandem MS. - *Quantitation*: ESI or APCI (good reproducibility). - *Rapid screening*: MALDI (fast acquisition). 3. **Instrument availability & cost** - EI and CI are standard in most GC‑MS labs. - ESI/APCI/APPI require LC‑MS systems. - MALDI needs a MALDI‑TOF instrument. 4. **Sensitivity & dynamic range** - ESI generally offers the best sensitivity for polar analytes. - MALDI excels for high‑molecular‑weight species but may have lower dynamic range. 5. **Sample preparation** - ESI/APCI: minimal prep, compatible with liquid samples. - EI/CI: requires derivatization for non‑volatile compounds. - MALDI: requires matrix deposition. ### Quick decision tree ``` ┌─ Is the analyte volatile? ──► Yes → Use EI or CI (GC‑MS) │ ├─ Is the analyte a large biomolecule? ──► Yes → Use ESI (LC‑MS) or MALDI (TOF) │ ├─ Is the analyte non‑polar and high‑MW? ──► Yes → Use MALDI or FI │ └─ Default → Use ESI (LC‑MS) for most polar, medium‑size molecules ``` --- **Bottom line:** There isn’t a single “best” ionisation method; the optimal choice depends on the analyte’s physical/chemical properties, the analytical goal (qualitative vs. quantitative), and the instrumentation at hand. For most routine LC‑MS work involving proteins, peptides, or polar metabolites, **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** is the go‑to method because of its softness, versatility, and compatibility with atmospheric pressure operation. For volatile organics, **Electron Impact (EI)** remains the gold standard. For large biomolecules or polymers, **MALDI** or **Field Ionisation (FI)** are preferred.
